name: Decibel level
description: Computes a power ratio expressed in decibels, using 10×log10(p/p0), where p is the measured intensity and p0 a reference. It converts a multiplicative ratio into a logarithmic scale.
notes: This 10×log form is for power or intensity ratios; amplitude ratios use 20×log instead. Every 10 dB corresponds to a tenfold change in power.

name: Wave speed (v = fλ)
description: Computes wave speed as frequency×wavelength, giving how fast a wave propagates in m/s from its frequency in hertz and wavelength in metres.
notes: Applies to any periodic wave in a uniform medium. Frequency in Hz and wavelength in m give speed in m/s; keep units consistent.

name: Angular frequency from period
description: Converts an oscillation period into angular frequency, the rate of phase change in radians per second. It divides one full cycle of 2π radians by the period t, so a shorter period yields a proportionally larger angular frequency.
notes: The period must be in seconds so the result comes out in rad/s. Angular frequency ω differs from ordinary frequency f by a factor of 2π (ω = 2πf).

name: Frequency from period
description: Converts a period into frequency by taking the reciprocal of the time for one full cycle. A period of 0.5 seconds corresponds to 2 cycles per second, or 2 hertz.
notes: The period must be in seconds so the frequency comes out in hertz. This gives ordinary frequency f, not angular frequency ω (which is 2π times larger).

name: Period from Frequency
description: Converts a frequency into the period of one cycle by taking its reciprocal. A frequency of 440 hertz corresponds to a period of about 0.00227 seconds per cycle.
notes: Frequency must be in hertz to yield the period in seconds. This is the exact inverse of the frequency-from-period relation.

name: Refractive Index (n=c/v)
description: Calculates the refractive index of a medium as the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum to its speed in the medium. Light slows in denser optical media, so a higher index means slower propagation.
notes: Both speeds must use the same unit; the result is dimensionless and at least 1 for ordinary media. It describes phase speed reduction, not absorption.

name: Snell's Law (refraction angle)
description: Uses Snell's law to find the angle of refraction when light passes from a medium of index n1 into one of index n2 at incidence angle theta1. Light bends toward the normal when entering a denser (higher-index) medium.
notes: Angles are in radians measured from the surface normal. If n1 sin(theta1) exceeds n2, total internal reflection occurs and no real refraction angle exists (arcsine undefined).

name: Thin Lens (image distance)
description: Solves the thin-lens equation for the image distance given the focal length and object distance. It locates where a lens forms an image, whether real (positive result) or virtual (negative result).
notes: Follows the sign convention where a positive focal length is a converging lens. If the object sits at the focal point, the denominator is zero and the image forms at infinity.

name: Magnification
description: Gives the transverse magnification of an optical system as the negative ratio of image distance to object distance. Its sign shows image orientation and its magnitude shows how much larger or smaller the image is.
notes: A negative result means an inverted image; a magnitude below 1 means the image is reduced. Use the same distance unit and consistent sign convention for both distances.

name: Lensmaker's Equation (focal length)
description: Uses the lensmaker's equation to find the focal length of a thin lens from its refractive index and the radii of curvature of its two surfaces. It links the lens shape and material to its converging or diverging power.
notes: Radii follow a sign convention (positive if the surface center of curvature is on the outgoing side). Assumes a thin lens in air; a positive result is a converging lens.

name: Mirror Equation (image distance)
description: Solves the mirror equation for the image distance of a curved mirror given its focal length and the object distance. It shows where a spherical mirror forms an image of an object.
notes: Uses the sign convention where a concave mirror has positive focal length. A negative image distance indicates a virtual image behind the mirror.

name: Sound Level (decibels)
description: Computes the sound intensity level in decibels as ten times the base-10 logarithm of the intensity relative to a reference intensity. The logarithmic scale compresses the huge range of audible intensities.
notes: The reference i0 is usually 1e-12 W/m², the threshold of hearing. A tenfold increase in intensity raises the level by 10 dB; both intensities must use the same unit.

name: Sound Intensity
description: Gives the sound intensity at distance r from a point source radiating power p uniformly in all directions, by spreading the power over the surface of a sphere of radius r. Intensity falls off as the inverse square of distance.
notes: Assumes a point source with no reflections or absorption in the medium. Doubling the distance cuts the intensity to a quarter; keep power in watts and distance in meters.

name: Doppler Effect (approaching)
description: Gives the frequency heard when a source and observer approach each other, shifting the source frequency upward. The observed frequency rises as the observer speed adds to and the source speed subtracts from the speed of sound in the ratio.
notes: All speeds are relative to the medium (still air) and must be positive for approach in this configuration. Valid only while source speed stays below the speed of sound.

name: Doppler Effect (receding)
description: Gives the frequency heard when a source and observer recede from each other, shifting the source frequency downward. The observer speed subtracts from and the source speed adds to the speed of sound in the ratio, lowering the observed pitch.
notes: All speeds are relative to the medium and taken positive for the receding case. It assumes motion along the line joining source and observer.

name: Diffraction Grating (angle)
description: Uses the diffraction grating equation to find the angle at which the m-th order maximum appears for light of a given wavelength and slit spacing. Longer wavelengths and higher orders diffract to larger angles.
notes: The slit spacing d is the distance between adjacent slits (inverse of lines per meter). No solution exists if m times wavelength exceeds d, since the arcsine argument would exceed 1.

name: Oscillator Wave Energy
description: Computes the total energy of a mechanical oscillator vibrating at frequency f with amplitude a, treating it as simple harmonic motion with angular frequency 2πf. The energy grows with the square of both frequency and amplitude.
notes: Frequency must be in hertz; it is converted internally to angular frequency. The result assumes undamped simple harmonic motion of the given mass.

name: Standing Wave Harmonic (string)
description: Gives the frequency of the n-th harmonic of a standing wave on a string fixed at both ends, from the wave speed and string length. The harmonics are integer multiples of the fundamental frequency (n = 1).
notes: This form assumes a string fixed at both ends (or a pipe open at both ends). Use the wave speed on the string, which generally differs from the speed of sound in air.

name: Speed of Sound in Air
description: Estimates the speed of sound in dry air as a linear function of temperature, starting from about 331 m/s at 0 degrees Celsius and rising roughly 0.6 m/s per degree. At 20 degrees it gives about 343 m/s.
notes: Temperature must be in degrees Celsius. This is a linear approximation valid near everyday temperatures; it ignores humidity and air pressure effects.

name: Angular Frequency
description: Converts an ordinary frequency in hertz into angular frequency in radians per second by multiplying by 2π. It expresses how many radians of phase the oscillation advances each second.
notes: Frequency must be in hertz (cycles per second). Angular frequency ω is 2π times larger than f; do not confuse the two in oscillation formulas.

name: Wave Number
description: Computes the angular wave number, the spatial frequency of a wave, as 2π divided by the wavelength. It gives the number of radians of phase per unit distance along the wave.
notes: This is the angular wave number in rad/m, not the spectroscopic 1/λ convention. Wavelength must be in meters; shorter wavelengths give larger wave numbers.

name: Frequency from Wave Speed
description: Finds the frequency of a wave from its propagation speed and wavelength by dividing the speed by the wavelength. For a fixed speed, shorter wavelengths correspond to higher frequencies.
notes: Use the wave speed in the same medium as the wavelength. This rearranges the basic relation v = f times wavelength; keep speed in m/s and wavelength in meters.

name: Wavelength from Speed & Frequency
description: Finds the wavelength of a wave by dividing its propagation speed by its frequency. Higher-frequency waves have shorter wavelengths when the speed is fixed.
notes: Use the wave speed in the medium of interest and frequency in hertz. This is the standard v = f times wavelength relation solved for wavelength.

name: Malus's Law
description: Gives the intensity of polarized light after passing through a polarizer, as the incident intensity times the square of the cosine of the angle between the light's polarization and the polarizer axis. Aligned axes transmit fully; crossed axes block all light.
notes: The angle theta must be in radians and is measured between the polarization direction and the transmission axis. It applies to already-polarized light, not unpolarized light.

name: Bragg's Law (wavelength)
description: Uses Bragg's law to find the wavelength that satisfies constructive interference for X-rays reflected from crystal planes spaced d apart at Bragg angle theta, for diffraction order n. It underlies X-ray crystallography.
notes: The angle theta is measured from the crystal plane surface, not the normal, and must be in radians. A valid reflection requires the wavelength to fit within 2d divided by n.

name: Beat Frequency
description: Gives the beat frequency produced when two waves of slightly different frequencies interfere, equal to the absolute difference of the two frequencies. It is the rate at which the combined sound swells and fades.
notes: Both frequencies must use the same unit; the absolute value keeps the result positive regardless of order. Beats are only perceptible when the two frequencies are close.

name: Lens Power
description: Computes the optical power of a lens as the reciprocal of its focal length. A shorter focal length yields greater power, expressed in diopters, so a 0.05 m focal length gives 20 D.
notes: Focal length must be entered in meters, not centimeters, for the result to be in diopters. Use a negative focal length for diverging (concave) lenses, which gives negative power.

name: Rayleigh Criterion (angular resolution)
description: Gives the smallest angular separation that a circular aperture can resolve, from diffraction theory. Two point sources closer than 1.22×wavelength/diameter blur together; the result is the limiting angle in radians.
notes: Wavelength and aperture diameter must share the same length unit (meters). The 1.22 factor applies to circular apertures; slits use a factor of 1. Smaller angle means finer resolving power.

name: Speed of Light in Medium
description: Calculates how fast light travels through a transparent medium by dividing the vacuum speed of light by the medium's refractive index. A higher index means slower light, so n=1.33 (water) gives about 2.26×10⁸ m/s.
notes: The refractive index is dimensionless and always at least 1 for ordinary media. This is phase speed; it does not exceed the vacuum value c because n≥1.

name: Photon Momentum
description: Determines the momentum carried by a single photon from its wavelength, using Planck's constant divided by wavelength. Shorter wavelengths carry more momentum; the result is in kg·m/s.
notes: Wavelength must be in meters. This is the de Broglie relation p=h/λ; equivalently p=E/c. Photon momentum is extremely small, so results are on the order of 10⁻²⁷ kg·m/s.

name: Fundamental Frequency of a String
description: Finds the lowest vibration frequency of a stretched string fixed at both ends, from its length, tension, and linear mass density. Higher tension or a shorter, lighter string raises the pitch; the result is in hertz.
notes: Linear density is mass per unit length (kg/m), not total mass. This gives only the fundamental; harmonics are integer multiples. Assumes an ideal, uniform, perfectly flexible string.

name: Relativistic Doppler Effect
description: Gives the observed frequency for relative motion along the line of sight, f = f0·√((1 + β)/(1 − β)), where β = v/c. As written, a positive β corresponds to approach and a blueshift.
notes: β is the speed as a fraction of c and must be between −1 and 1; use a negative value for recession (redshift). This longitudinal form ignores the purely transverse Doppler effect.

name: Magnifier Angular Magnification
description: Gives the angular magnification of a simple magnifier with the image at the near point, M = 25/f, where f is the focal length in centimetres and 25 cm is the standard near-point distance.
notes: The focal length must be in centimetres because 25 is the near-point distance in centimetres. This assumes a relaxed eye viewing at the conventional 25 cm near point.

name: Telescope Magnification
description: Computes the angular magnification of a refracting telescope in normal adjustment, M = fo/fe, the ratio of the objective focal length to the eyepiece focal length. Longer objectives or shorter eyepieces give more magnification.
notes: Both focal lengths must be in the same unit so the ratio is dimensionless. This assumes the telescope is focused for a relaxed eye with the final image at infinity.

name: Compound Microscope Magnification
description: Gives the total magnification of a compound microscope, (L/fo)·(25/fe), the product of the objective magnification set by the tube length L and the eyepiece magnification. It multiplies two stages of enlargement.
notes: All lengths must be in centimetres to match the 25 cm near-point term. L is the optical tube length between the focal points, and the eye is assumed relaxed.

name: Numerical Aperture
description: Computes the numerical aperture NA = n·sin θ of an optical system, where n is the refractive index of the medium and θ is the half-angle of the maximum cone of light accepted. Larger NA means finer resolving power.
notes: The half-angle must be in radians. NA is dimensionless and cannot exceed the medium's refractive index, which is why immersion media with n above 1 raise the achievable aperture.

name: Rayleigh Angular Resolution
description: Gives the smallest angular separation resolvable by a circular aperture, θ = 1.22·λ/d, from the Rayleigh criterion. Longer wavelengths or smaller apertures give a coarser (larger) resolution angle.
notes: Wavelength and aperture diameter must share the same length unit so the result is in radians. The factor 1.22 is specific to a circular aperture and reflects its diffraction pattern.

name: Brewster's Angle
description: Computes Brewster's angle, θ = arctan(n2/n1), the angle of incidence at which light reflected from a boundary is completely polarised. n1 is the incident medium index and n2 the refracting medium index.
notes: The refractive indices are dimensionless and their order matters; swapping them gives the complementary situation. The result is in radians and is measured from the surface normal.

name: Thin-Film Constructive Thickness (min)
description: Gives the minimum film thickness λ/(2·n) for constructive interference in reflection when there is a half-wave phase shift at only one surface. λ is the vacuum wavelength and n the film's refractive index.
notes: This specific form assumes a single half-wave phase shift (a low-high-low index stack) and near-normal incidence. The vacuum wavelength is divided by n because the wave is shorter inside the film.

name: Double-Slit Fringe Spacing
description: Computes the spacing between adjacent bright fringes in a double-slit interference pattern, Δy = λ·L/d, where L is the slit-to-screen distance and d the slit separation. Wider slit separation gives closer fringes.
notes: This small-angle approximation assumes the screen is far from the slits (L much greater than d). All lengths must use the same unit so the fringe spacing comes out in metres.

name: Combined Lens Power (in contact)
description: Gives the combined optical power of two thin lenses in contact, P = p1 + p2, since their powers add directly. This determines the effective focal length of the pair.
notes: This simple sum holds only for thin lenses placed in contact with negligible separation; a finite gap requires a correction term. Both powers are in dioptres, with diverging lenses entered as negative.

name: f-Number
description: Computes the f-number N = f/d of a lens, the ratio of focal length to aperture diameter. A larger f-number means a smaller aperture, less light gathered, and greater depth of field.
notes: Focal length and aperture diameter must share the same unit so the result is dimensionless. The light-gathering area scales as 1/N², so doubling N cuts the light to a quarter.

name: Critical Angle (total internal reflection)
description: Computes the critical angle θ = arcsin(n2/n1) beyond which light in a denser medium (index n1) undergoes total internal reflection at a boundary with a rarer medium (index n2). Above this angle no light is transmitted.
notes: It requires n1 greater than n2 so the ratio is below one; otherwise no critical angle exists. The result is in radians and measured from the surface normal.

name: Single-Slit First Minimum Angle
description: Gives the angle to the first diffraction minimum of a single slit, θ = arcsin(λ/a), where λ is the wavelength and a the slit width. Narrower slits spread the diffraction pattern to larger angles.
notes: Wavelength and slit width must share a unit, and λ/a must not exceed one. The result is in radians and marks the first dark fringe, not a bright one.

name: Bragg Diffraction Angle
description: Computes the Bragg angle θ = arcsin(m·λ/(2·d)) at which X-rays of wavelength λ diffract constructively from crystal planes spaced by d. The condition is m·λ = 2·d·sin θ.
notes: The angle is measured between the incident beam and the crystal plane, not the normal. The argument m·λ/(2·d) must not exceed one, and wavelength and spacing must share a unit.

name: Fresnel Reflectance (normal incidence)
description: Computes the fraction of light intensity reflected at a flat interface between two media at normal incidence, from their refractive indices n1 and n2. The dimensionless result ranges from 0 to 1, so 0.04 means 4 percent of the power is reflected.
notes: Valid only for normal (perpendicular) incidence and non-absorbing media; at oblique angles use the full Fresnel equations. The result is symmetric in n1 and n2, and assumes real refractive indices.

name: Speed of Sound (Ideal Gas)
description: Gives the speed of sound in an ideal gas, as the square root of the heat capacity ratio times the specific gas constant times absolute temperature. The result in meters per second depends only on the gas type and its temperature.
notes: Temperature must be absolute (kelvin), and the specific gas constant is for the particular gas, not the universal constant. Sound speed rises with the square root of temperature and is independent of pressure.

name: Fluid Sound Speed (Bulk Modulus)
description: Computes the speed of sound in a liquid or solid, as the square root of the bulk modulus divided by density. The result in meters per second reflects how fast pressure waves propagate through the medium.
notes: Use the adiabatic bulk modulus for acoustic waves. Stiffer (higher bulk modulus) or lighter media transmit sound faster; this form suits nearly incompressible fluids rather than gases.

name: Lensmaker's Equation (thick lens)
description: Computes the optical power (reciprocal focal length) of a thick lens from its refractive index, the two surface radii of curvature, and the center thickness, using the full lensmaker's equation. The thickness term corrects the thin-lens result for finite lens depth.
notes: Follows a sign convention for radii (positive if the center of curvature is to the right). Assumes the lens is in air; the reciprocal of the power gives the focal length.

name: Total Internal Reflection Critical Angle
description: Gives the critical angle for total internal reflection at an interface, the angle of incidence in the denser medium beyond which all light is reflected, as the arcsine of the ratio of the rarer to the denser refractive index.
notes: Requires n1 greater than n2 (light going from dense to rare medium); otherwise total internal reflection does not occur. The result is in radians measured from the surface normal.

name: Two-Lens System Focal Length (separated)
description: Computes the effective focal length of two thin lenses separated by a distance, using the combined-power formula. The system power is the sum of the individual powers minus a coupling term proportional to the separation.
notes: Valid for thin lenses in air separated along a common axis. The effective focal length is measured from the system's principal planes, not from either lens.

name: Anti-Reflection Coating Thickness (quarter-wave)
description: Gives the minimum physical thickness of a single-layer quarter-wave anti-reflection coating, equal to the wavelength divided by four times the coating's refractive index. At this thickness reflected waves interfere destructively.
notes: Wavelength is the value in vacuum; dividing by the index converts to the optical quarter-wave. Optimal cancellation also requires the coating index near the geometric mean of the two surrounding media.

name: Young's Double-Slit Fringe Width
description: Computes the spacing between adjacent bright (or dark) fringes in a Young's double-slit interference pattern, equal to the wavelength times the screen distance divided by the slit separation. Wider fringes result from longer wavelength, farther screens, or closer slits.
notes: Valid in the small-angle (paraxial) approximation where the screen distance greatly exceeds the slit separation. All lengths use the same unit; wavelength is in vacuum or the surrounding medium.

name: Single-Slit Diffraction Minimum Angle
description: Gives the angle of the first intensity minimum in single-slit Fraunhofer diffraction, as the arcsine of the wavelength divided by the slit width. Narrower slits spread the diffraction pattern to larger angles.
notes: This is the first-order minimum; higher orders occur at m times wavelength over width. Requires wavelength no larger than the slit width for a real angle. Result is in radians.

name: Grating Resolving Power
description: Computes the chromatic resolving power of a diffraction grating, equal to the diffraction order times the number of illuminated lines. It gives the ratio of wavelength to the smallest resolvable wavelength difference.
notes: N counts only the grating lines actually illuminated by the beam, not the total ruled lines. Higher orders and wider illumination improve resolution.

name: Hyperfocal Distance (photographic)
description: Computes the photographic hyperfocal distance, the focus distance at which everything from half that distance to infinity appears acceptably sharp. It is the focal length squared divided by (f-number times circle of confusion), plus the focal length.
notes: The circle of confusion sets the acceptable blur and depends on sensor size and viewing conditions. Focal length, circle of confusion, and result use the same length unit.

name: Newton's Rings Radius (dark)
description: Gives the radius of the m-th dark ring in a Newton's rings interference pattern, equal to the square root of the ring number times the wavelength times the lens radius of curvature. The rings arise from interference in the thin air gap between a curved lens and a flat plate.
notes: Applies to reflected light with an air gap, where the center is dark; m counts dark rings from the center. Wavelength is that in the gap medium.

name: Fresnel Reflectivity at Normal Incidence
description: Computes the fraction of light intensity reflected at a boundary between two media at normal incidence, given by the squared ratio of the index difference to the index sum. It quantifies reflection loss at an uncoated interface.
notes: Valid only for normal (perpendicular) incidence and non-absorbing dielectrics. The result is a reflectance between 0 and 1; the transmitted fraction is one minus this value.

name: Abbe Number
description: Computes the Abbe number, a measure of an optical material's dispersion, from its refractive indices at the d, F, and C spectral lines. A high Abbe number indicates low dispersion (less chromatic spreading).
notes: Uses the standard Fraunhofer lines (d ~587.6 nm, F ~486.1 nm, C ~656.3 nm). Dimensionless; larger values mean weaker wavelength dependence of the index.

name: Airy Disk Radius
description: Gives the radius of the Airy disk, the central bright spot of a diffraction-limited focused image, equal to 1.22 times the wavelength times the focal length divided by the aperture diameter. It sets the smallest resolvable spot size of an optical system.
notes: This is the radius to the first dark ring; the factor 1.22 comes from the first zero of the Airy pattern. Assumes a circular aperture and diffraction-limited optics.

name: Transverse Magnification (thin lens)
description: Computes the transverse (lateral) magnification of a thin lens, equal to minus the image distance divided by the object distance. Its magnitude gives the height ratio of image to object and its sign indicates image orientation.
notes: A negative result means an inverted (real) image; positive means upright (virtual). Distances follow the standard sign convention and share the same unit.

name: Longitudinal Magnification (thin lens)
description: Gives the longitudinal (axial) magnification of a thin lens, equal to the square of the ratio of image to object distance. It describes how depth along the optical axis is scaled and equals the square of the transverse magnification.
notes: Because it is the transverse magnification squared, longitudinal magnification is always positive and grows rapidly for large transverse magnification, distorting depth.

name: Spherical Mirror Focal Length
description: Gives the focal length of a spherical mirror, equal to half its radius of curvature. The mirror focuses parallel rays at this distance in the paraxial approximation.
notes: Valid in the paraxial (small-angle) limit; wide apertures suffer spherical aberration. Sign of the radius follows the mirror sign convention (concave versus convex).

name: Prism Refractive Index (minimum deviation)
description: Computes the refractive index of a prism from its apex angle and the angle of minimum deviation, using the standard minimum-deviation relation. This is the classic method for measuring a material's refractive index with a spectrometer.
notes: Both angles are in radians and the measurement must be taken at the minimum-deviation condition, where the ray passes symmetrically through the prism.

name: Thin-Film Optical Path Difference
description: Computes the optical path difference between rays reflected from the top and bottom of a thin film, equal to twice the film index times the thickness times the cosine of the refraction angle. It determines the condition for constructive or destructive interference.
notes: The refraction angle is the angle inside the film, not the angle of incidence. A half-wavelength phase shift on reflection may add to this path difference when applying interference conditions.

name: Cauchy's Equation (refractive index)
description: Gives the refractive index of a transparent material as a function of wavelength using Cauchy's two-term empirical equation, index equals A plus B over wavelength squared. It captures normal dispersion, where index rises toward shorter wavelengths.
notes: Wavelength and the coefficient B must use consistent units (here micrometres and micrometres squared). Valid only in the material's transparent region away from absorption bands.

name: Sellmeier Equation (single term)
description: Computes the refractive index of a transparent material from a single-term Sellmeier equation, taking the square root of one plus B times wavelength squared over (wavelength squared minus C). It models dispersion more accurately than Cauchy's equation across a wide range.
notes: Wavelength and coefficient C use squared-micrometre units; C is a resonance wavelength squared. Valid away from the resonance where the denominator would vanish.

name: Abbe Diffraction Limit
description: Gives the Abbe diffraction limit, the smallest resolvable feature size in a microscope, equal to the wavelength divided by twice the numerical aperture. It sets the classical resolution bound of far-field optical imaging.
notes: Numerical aperture combines the medium index and the half-angle of light collection. Shorter wavelengths and higher numerical aperture improve resolution; super-resolution techniques can surpass this bound.

name: Apparent Depth (refraction)
description: Computes the apparent depth of an object seen through a flat refracting interface, equal to the real depth times the ratio of the viewer's medium index to the object's medium index. It explains why objects underwater appear shallower than they truly are.
notes: Valid for near-normal (paraxial) viewing through a flat interface. When viewing from air into water the apparent depth is less than the real depth.

name: Beer-Lambert Transmittance
description: Gives the fraction of light intensity that passes through an absorbing medium, exp(-alpha·l). With absorption coefficient alpha and path length l, the result runs from 1 (no absorption) toward 0 as the product alpha·l grows.
notes: alpha and l must use reciprocal units (here 1/m and m) so alpha·l is dimensionless. The output is a bare ratio between 0 and 1, not a percentage; multiply by 100 for percent transmittance.

name: Refracting Surface Power
description: Computes the optical power of a single refracting surface, (n2-n1)/R, from the indices before and after the surface and its radius of curvature R. The result in diopters (1/m) shows how strongly the surface bends light.
notes: Follow a sign convention for R: it is positive when the center of curvature lies on the outgoing side. A larger index difference or smaller radius gives greater power.

name: Diffraction Grating Angle (m-th order)
description: Solves the grating equation for the diffraction angle of the m-th order, asin(m·lambda/d), where lambda is the wavelength and d the grating pitch. The result in radians is the angle at which that order constructively interferes.
notes: The order exists only if m·lambda/d ≤ 1; otherwise the arcsine is undefined (order not diffracted). Assumes normal incidence and angle measured from the grating normal.

name: Grating Angular Dispersion
description: Gives the angular dispersion of a diffraction grating, m/(d·cos(theta)), the rate at which diffraction angle changes with wavelength for order m at diffraction angle theta. Larger values mean wavelengths spread apart more strongly.
notes: theta must be in radians. The value diverges as theta approaches 90 degrees because cos(theta) tends to zero; it represents dtheta/dlambda, not the angle itself.

name: Fraunhofer Distance
description: Estimates the Fraunhofer (far-field) distance, 2·D²/lambda, beyond which diffraction from an aperture of size D at wavelength lambda is well described by far-field theory. The result is the minimum distance for far-field conditions.
notes: D and lambda share the same length unit so the result comes out in meters. This is an order-of-magnitude criterion; closer than this distance the near-field (Fresnel) treatment applies.

name: Fresnel Number
description: Computes the Fresnel number, a²/(lambda·L), a dimensionless measure comparing aperture radius a, wavelength lambda, and observation distance L. It indicates whether diffraction is in the near-field (large N) or far-field (small N) regime.
notes: All lengths must use consistent units so the result is dimensionless. N of order 1 marks the transition; N much less than 1 corresponds to Fraunhofer (far-field) diffraction.

name: Numerical Aperture from f-number
description: Approximates the numerical aperture of a lens from its f-number, NA = 1/(2·N). It relates the light-gathering cone of an optical system to the familiar photographic f-stop N.
notes: This is the paraxial small-angle approximation valid in air; for fast (low N) lenses the exact form NA = 1/(2·sqrt(N²+... )) differs. Larger f-number means smaller NA and less light.

name: Symmetric Biconvex Focal Length
description: Gives the focal length of a thin symmetric biconvex lens, R/(2·(n-1)), where both surfaces share radius R and n is the glass index. It follows from the lensmaker equation with equal and opposite surface radii.
notes: Valid in the thin-lens approximation and for a lens in air. Requires n greater than 1; as n approaches 1 the focal length grows without bound (weak lens).

name: Illuminance Inverse-Square Law
description: Computes illuminance on a surface from a point source, I/r², where I is luminous intensity in candela and r the distance. Illuminance in lux falls off as the inverse square of distance.
notes: Valid for a point source and a surface facing the source directly (normal incidence). For tilted surfaces multiply by cos of the incidence angle.

name: Illuminance (Lambert's Cosine Law)
description: Computes illuminance on a tilted surface, I·cos(theta)/r², combining the inverse-square law with Lambert's cosine law for incidence angle theta. It gives the lux received when the surface normal makes angle theta with the incoming light.
notes: theta is in radians, measured from the surface normal. At theta = 0 it reduces to the plain inverse-square law; illuminance vanishes at grazing incidence (theta = pi/2).

name: Michelson Contrast (visibility)
description: Computes the Michelson contrast (fringe visibility), (Imax-Imin)/(Imax+Imin), from the maximum and minimum intensities of a pattern. The result ranges from 0 (uniform) to 1 (fully modulated).
notes: Imax and Imin should be non-negative intensities with Imax ≥ Imin; the denominator must not be zero. This normalized measure is preferred for periodic patterns and interference fringes.

name: Rayleigh Scattering Intensity
description: Gives the relative Rayleigh scattering intensity, I0·(l0/lambda)⁴, showing the strong inverse fourth-power dependence on wavelength. Shorter wavelengths scatter far more, explaining why the sky is blue.
notes: l0 and lambda must share the same length unit. Valid only for particles much smaller than the wavelength; the result is relative to reference intensity I0 at wavelength l0.

name: Acceptance Half-Angle from NA
description: Inverts the numerical-aperture relation to find the acceptance half-angle, asin(NA/n), for a given numerical aperture NA in a medium of index n. The result in radians is the half-angle of the accepted light cone.
notes: Requires NA ≤ n so the arcsine is defined; NA/n greater than 1 has no real angle. The result is the half-angle, so double it for the full acceptance cone.

name: Newton's Lens Equation (image)
description: Uses Newton's form of the thin-lens equation, f²/xobj, to give the image distance measured from the rear focal point when the object sits distance xobj in front of the front focal point. Here f is the focal length.
notes: Distances are measured from the focal points, not the lens, and follow a sign convention. As the object approaches the focal point (xobj to 0), the image distance grows without bound.

name: Thin Prism Deviation Angle
description: Gives the deviation angle of light through a thin prism, (n-1)·A, from the prism index n and small apex angle A. It is the angle by which a ray is bent, independent of incidence angle for a thin prism.
notes: A is in radians and must be small for this linear approximation to hold. Because n varies with wavelength, the deviation differs by color, producing dispersion.

name: Etendue (optical throughput)
description: Computes the etendue (optical throughput), n²·A·Omega, from medium index n, source area A, and solid angle Omega. It quantifies how much light an optical system can collect and is conserved along an ideal system.
notes: Omega is in steradians and A in square meters, giving units of m² sr. Etendue can only stay equal or increase through a real system; it never decreases (brightness conservation).

name: Optical Path Length
description: Computes the optical path length, n·d, the product of refractive index n and the geometric length d traveled. It is the equivalent distance in vacuum that produces the same phase accumulation.
notes: OPL, not geometric length, governs interference and phase differences. In a medium with n greater than 1 the optical path always exceeds the physical distance d.

name: Faraday Rotation Angle (Verdet)
description: Computes the Faraday rotation angle, V·B·Lp, by which the polarization plane rotates when light passes through a medium of Verdet constant V along path Lp in a magnetic flux density B parallel to the beam.
notes: Only the field component along the propagation direction contributes. The rotation sign follows the sign of V and the field direction; a negative V rotates oppositely.

name: Photon Flux (photons per second)
description: Computes the photon flux, P·lambda/(h·c), the number of photons per second in an optical beam of power P at wavelength lambda. It divides the total power by the energy of a single photon (h·c/lambda).
notes: All quantities in SI (W, m, J·s, m/s) yield photons per second. Longer wavelengths carry less energy per photon, so a given power corresponds to more photons per second.

name: Fiber Acceptance Angle
description: Gives the acceptance half-angle of a step-index optical fiber, asin(sqrt(n1²-n2²)/n0), from the core index n1, cladding index n2, and external medium index n0. Light within this angle is guided by total internal reflection.
notes: Requires n1 greater than n2 for a real result. n0 is the launch medium (often air, n0 = 1); the result is the half-angle of the acceptance cone in radians.

name: Fiber Numerical Aperture
description: Computes the numerical aperture of a step-index fiber, sqrt(n1²-n2²), from the core index n1 and cladding index n2. It sets the light-gathering ability and the acceptance cone of the fiber.
notes: Requires n1 greater than n2. This dimensionless NA assumes launch from air; a larger core-cladding index difference gives a wider acceptance cone.

name: Fiber V-number (normalized frequency)
description: Computes the fiber V-number (normalized frequency), 2·pi·a·NA/lambda, from core radius a, numerical aperture NA, and wavelength lambda. This dimensionless parameter governs how many modes the fiber supports.
notes: a and lambda share the same length unit. Single-mode operation requires V less than about 2.405 (the first Bessel zero); above it the fiber becomes multimode.

name: Step-Index Fiber Mode Count
description: Estimates the number of guided modes in a step-index multimode fiber, V²/2, from the V-number V. It approximates the total count of modes (including polarizations) that the fiber can carry.
notes: This approximation holds only for large V (strongly multimode fibers); near single-mode it overestimates. The result should be treated as an integer count.

name: Optical Cavity Q-factor
description: Computes the quality factor of an optical cavity, 2·pi·f·tauph, from the optical frequency f and the photon lifetime tauph. A higher Q means light is stored longer relative to its oscillation period.
notes: tauph is the 1/e energy decay time inside the cavity, in seconds. Q is dimensionless and equal to 2·pi times the number of optical cycles before the energy decays by 1/e.

name: Fabry-Perot Free Spectral Range
description: Computes the free spectral range of a Fabry-Perot cavity, c/(2·n·L), the frequency spacing between adjacent longitudinal modes for a cavity of length L filled with medium index n. It sets how far apart the transmission peaks lie in frequency.
notes: The result is in hertz (frequency spacing), not wavelength. n·L is the optical path of one pass; a longer or higher-index cavity gives a smaller FSR.

name: Fabry-Perot Finesse
description: Computes the finesse of a Fabry-Perot cavity, pi·sqrt(R)/(1-R), from the mirror reflectance R. Finesse is the ratio of the free spectral range to the resonance linewidth, so higher values mean sharper transmission peaks.
notes: Assumes equal, lossless mirrors of reflectance R (a fraction between 0 and 1). As R approaches 1 the finesse rises steeply; the denominator (1-R) must not be zero.

name: Gaussian Beam Rayleigh Range
description: Computes the Rayleigh range of a Gaussian beam, pi·w0²/lambda, from the beam waist radius w0 and wavelength lambda. It is the distance from the waist over which the beam cross-sectional area doubles.
notes: w0 and lambda share the same length unit. The beam stays roughly collimated within one Rayleigh range of the waist and diverges appreciably beyond it.

name: Gaussian Beam Divergence Angle
description: Computes the far-field divergence half-angle of a Gaussian beam, lambda/(pi·w0), from the wavelength lambda and beam waist w0. It is the asymptotic half-angle at which the beam spreads far from the waist.
notes: The result is in radians and is the half-angle. A tighter waist (smaller w0) gives a larger divergence, reflecting the diffraction limit.

name: Gaussian Beam Radius at Distance
description: Computes the Gaussian beam radius at distance z from the waist, w0·sqrt(1+(z/zR)²), using the waist w0 and Rayleigh range zR. It describes the hyperbolic growth of the beam as it propagates away from focus.
notes: z is measured from the waist and zR is the Rayleigh range in the same units. At z = zR the radius equals sqrt(2)·w0; far from the waist growth becomes linear.

name: Focused Gaussian Beam Waist
description: Estimates the focused spot radius of a Gaussian beam, lambda·f/(pi·w), when an input beam of radius w passes through a lens of focal length f at wavelength lambda. It gives the diffraction-limited waist at the focus.
notes: Valid when the input beam fills the lens and its waist is at the lens (far-field focusing). A larger input radius w produces a smaller, tighter focal spot.

name: Group Index (from dispersion slope)
description: Computes the group index of a medium, n - lambda·(dn/dlambda), from the phase index n, wavelength lambda, and the index dispersion slope dn/dlambda. The group index governs the speed of a pulse envelope.
notes: dndl is dn/dlambda in units of 1/m and is usually negative in normal dispersion, making the group index exceed the phase index. Consistent length units are required.

name: Group Velocity (from group index)
description: Computes the group velocity, c/ng, at which a pulse envelope travels through a medium of group index ng. It is the speed of energy or information transport, generally slower than the phase velocity.
notes: Uses the group index ng, not the phase index. In normal media ng exceeds 1, so the group velocity is less than the vacuum speed of light c.

name: Fiber Chromatic Dispersion Delay
description: Computes the pulse broadening from chromatic dispersion, D·L·dlambda, over a fiber of length L with dispersion parameter D and source spectral width dlambda. It gives the spread in arrival time between spectral components.
notes: D is per unit length per unit wavelength (s/m²); with L in meters and dlambda in meters the result is a time in seconds. The broadening scales linearly with both length and spectral width.

name: Fiber Attenuation (dB)
description: Computes optical attenuation in decibels, 10·log10(Pin/Pout), from input power Pin and output power Pout. It expresses the total power loss of a fiber link on a logarithmic scale.
notes: log here is base 10 and the 10 factor applies because these are power (not amplitude) ratios. A positive value means loss (Pin greater than Pout); the two powers must share the same unit.

name: Fiber Loss Coefficient (dB/km)
description: Computes the per-length loss coefficient of a fiber, (10/L)·log10(Pin/Pout), from length L and the input and output powers. It normalizes total attenuation to a loss rate in decibels per kilometer.
notes: L is in kilometers so the result is dB/km. This assumes uniform loss along the fiber; connector or splice losses would inflate the apparent per-length coefficient.

name: Photodiode Responsivity
description: Computes photodiode responsivity, eta·q·lambda/(h·c), the ratio of generated photocurrent to incident optical power, from quantum efficiency eta, charge q, wavelength lambda, and constants h and c. The result is in amperes per watt.
notes: eta is a fraction between 0 and 1. Responsivity rises with wavelength for fixed efficiency, but real detectors lose efficiency near their band-gap cutoff.

name: Laser Threshold Gain
description: Computes the threshold gain of a laser, alpha + (1/(2·L))·ln(1/(R1·R2)), summing internal loss alpha and the mirror (output-coupling) loss of a cavity of length L with mirror reflectances R1 and R2. Gain must reach this value for lasing.
notes: R1 and R2 are fractions between 0 and 1; the term ln(1/(R1·R2)) is the round-trip mirror loss spread over the cavity length. Lower reflectances raise the threshold gain.

name: Photon Energy (eV)
description: Computes photon energy in electronvolts, h·c/(lambda·q), from Planck's constant h, speed of light c, wavelength lambda, and elementary charge q. Dividing the joule energy h·c/lambda by q converts it to eV.
notes: lambda in meters gives energy in electronvolts. A useful check: energy times wavelength is about 1.24 eV·um, so 1.55 um corresponds to roughly 0.8 eV.

name: Fiber Bragg Grating Wavelength
description: Computes the Bragg wavelength of a fiber Bragg grating, 2·neff·L, from the effective mode index neff and the grating period L. It is the wavelength strongly reflected by the periodic index modulation.
notes: L is the physical grating period, not its length; the result is a wavelength in the same length unit. This first-order Bragg condition assumes normal in-fiber incidence.

name: Extinction Ratio (dB)
description: Computes the extinction ratio in decibels, 10·log10(P1/P0), the logarithmic ratio of the optical power in the ON state P1 to that in the OFF state P0. It measures how cleanly a modulator or transmitter separates the two signal levels.
notes: log is base 10 and both are optical powers, so the factor is 10. A higher value means better on/off contrast; P1 and P0 must use the same power unit.

name: Optical Amplifier Gain (dB)
description: Computes optical amplifier gain in decibels, 10·log10(Pout/Pin), from output power Pout and input power Pin. It expresses the power amplification of a device such as an EDFA on a logarithmic scale.
notes: log is base 10 with a factor of 10 for power ratios. A positive value indicates gain (Pout greater than Pin); the two powers must share the same unit.

name: Shot Noise Current (RMS)
description: Computes the RMS shot-noise current, sqrt(2·q·I·B), from elementary charge q, average current I, and detection bandwidth B. It gives the fundamental current fluctuation arising from the discrete nature of charge.
notes: B is the noise-equivalent bandwidth in hertz. The noise grows as the square root of both the average current and bandwidth, so widening bandwidth raises noise more slowly than linearly.

name: Wien Displacement Law (frequency)
description: Computes the peak emission frequency of a blackbody, alpha·T, from the Wien frequency constant alpha and absolute temperature T. It locates the frequency of maximum spectral radiance in the frequency-form Planck spectrum.
notes: T is absolute temperature in kelvin. This is the frequency-domain Wien peak, which differs from the wavelength-domain peak converted by c/lambda (the peaks are not simply related).

name: Coherence Length
description: Computes the coherence length of light, lambda²/dlambda, from the center wavelength lambda and spectral width dlambda. It is the propagation distance over which the wave maintains a predictable phase relationship.
notes: lambda and dlambda share the same length unit; a narrower spectral width gives a longer coherence length. This is an approximate measure derived from the wavelength-frequency relation.

name: Coherence Time
description: Computes the coherence time, 1/dnu, the reciprocal of the spectral linewidth dnu. It is the time interval over which the light wave stays phase-correlated with itself.
notes: dnu is the linewidth in hertz, giving the coherence time in seconds. A narrower linewidth yields a longer coherence time; multiplying by the speed of light gives the coherence length.

name: Nonlinear Kerr Phase Shift
description: Computes the nonlinear (Kerr) phase shift, 2·pi·n2·I·L/lambda, accumulated by light of intensity I over length L in a medium with nonlinear index n2 at wavelength lambda. It quantifies self-phase modulation from the intensity-dependent index.
notes: n2 is in m²/W and I in W/m² so their product is dimensionless per unit length. The phase shift grows linearly with intensity and length, driving effects like self-phase modulation.

name: Multimode Fiber Modal Dispersion
description: Estimates modal dispersion in a step-index multimode fiber, n1·L·delta/c, the pulse spread from different mode path lengths, using core index n1, fiber length L, relative index difference delta, and speed of light c. The result is the delay between fastest and slowest modes.
notes: delta is the fractional core-cladding index difference (dimensionless). This is a step-index estimate; graded-index fibers reduce modal dispersion by orders of magnitude.

name: Purcell Factor
description: Computes the Purcell factor, (3/(4·pi²))·(lambda/n)³·Q/V, the enhancement of spontaneous emission rate for an emitter in a resonant cavity, from wavelength lambda, mode index n, cavity Q-factor, and mode volume V. Values above 1 mean accelerated emission.
notes: lambda/n is the wavelength inside the medium, cubed against the mode volume V in m³. High Q and small mode volume give large enhancement; assumes the emitter is on resonance and optimally placed.

name: Real Beam Divergence (M-squared)
description: Computes the divergence half-angle of a real (non-ideal) laser beam, M2·lambda/(pi·w0), scaling the ideal Gaussian divergence by the beam quality factor M². Here lambda is the wavelength and w0 the beam waist.
notes: M2 is dimensionless and at least 1; M2 = 1 recovers the ideal diffraction-limited Gaussian beam. The result is a half-angle in radians, larger for poorer beam quality.

name: Photodiode Quantum Efficiency
description: Converts a photodiode responsivity R (A/W) at wavelength lambda into external quantum efficiency, the average number of collected electrons per incident photon. It computes R*h*c/(q*lambda), a dimensionless ratio between 0 and 1 for an ideal detector.
notes: Wavelength must be in meters and R in A/W; the result is a fraction, not a percent. Values above 1 indicate gain (e.g. avalanche) or inconsistent inputs.

name: Dispersion Length (soliton)
description: Gives the characteristic dispersion length of an optical pulse in a fiber, the propagation distance over which group-velocity dispersion appreciably broadens a pulse of width T0. It is T0 squared divided by the magnitude of the GVD parameter beta2.
notes: T0 is the 1/e half-width, not the FWHM; convert accordingly. The absolute value is used, so the sign of beta2 (normal vs anomalous) does not change the length.

name: Nonlinear Length
description: Computes the nonlinear length of an optical fiber, the distance over which the Kerr effect accumulates one radian of nonlinear phase shift for a beam of peak power P. It equals the reciprocal of the product of the nonlinear coefficient gamma and P.
notes: Uses peak power, not average power; for pulses these differ greatly. Comparing this length with the dispersion length classifies the propagation regime (dispersive vs nonlinear).

name: Soliton Order
description: Returns the soliton order N of a pulse in a nonlinear fiber, the ratio that determines whether it forms a fundamental (N near 1) or higher-order soliton. It is the square root of gamma*P*T0 squared divided by the magnitude of beta2.
notes: Requires anomalous dispersion (beta2 negative) for soliton formation; the absolute value hides this, so verify the sign. N equals the square root of the ratio of dispersion length to nonlinear length.

name: Etalon FSR (wavelength)
description: Calculates the free spectral range of an etalon expressed in wavelength, the spacing between adjacent transmission peaks. It is lambda squared divided by twice the product of the medium index n and the cavity length L.
notes: Valid for near-normal incidence and holds only near the reference wavelength since the FSR itself depends on lambda. Length L is the physical cavity length in meters.

name: Confocal Parameter (Gaussian beam)
description: Gives the confocal parameter of a Gaussian beam, twice the Rayleigh range, over which the beam stays near its minimum size. It equals 2*pi times the beam waist w0 squared, divided by the wavelength lambda.
notes: Assumes a diffraction-limited fundamental Gaussian mode in a uniform medium; use the wavelength inside the medium. The waist w0 is the 1/e^2 intensity radius, not the diameter.

name: Photons per Pulse
description: Computes the number of photons contained in an optical pulse of energy Ep at wavelength lambda, by dividing the pulse energy by the single-photon energy h*c/lambda. The result is a dimensionless photon count.
notes: Assumes a single wavelength; broadband pulses need spectral integration. Energy in joules and wavelength in meters give the correct count, which is typically a very large number.

name: Doppler Broadening Linewidth
description: Calculates the Doppler-broadened full-width-at-half-maximum linewidth of a spectral transition in a thermal gas at temperature T. It scales the transition frequency nu0 by the square root of 8*ln(2)*kB*T/m over the speed of light.
notes: Assumes a Maxwell-Boltzmann velocity distribution; m is the mass of a single atom in kilograms. This gives the Gaussian FWHM, not the standard deviation or half-width.

name: Polarization Beat Length
description: Gives the polarization beat length in a birefringent fiber, the distance over which the two orthogonal polarization modes accumulate a 2*pi relative phase and the state of polarization repeats. It is the wavelength lambda divided by the birefringence dn.
notes: Birefringence dn is the dimensionless difference between the two mode indices. Shorter beat length means stronger polarization-maintaining behavior against external perturbations.

name: Slab Waveguide Cutoff Wavelength
description: Estimates the cutoff wavelength of mode m in a symmetric slab waveguide with core thickness d, above which that mode no longer propagates. It is 2*d times the square root of the index difference n1 squared minus n2 squared, divided by the mode order m.
notes: Applies to a symmetric step-index slab; the square-root term is the numerical aperture. Requires core index n1 greater than cladding index n2, and m a positive integer.

name: Optical Power in dBm
description: Converts optical power in milliwatts to the logarithmic dBm scale, P(dBm) = 10*log10(P_mW), the standard absolute power unit used throughout fiber-optic and telecom systems.
notes: 0 dBm corresponds to exactly 1 mW; P_mW must be positive. dBm values can be added and subtracted like decibels when combining losses and gains along a link.

name: Laser Output Power Above Threshold
description: Estimates a laser diode's optical output power above lasing threshold, P_out = eta_slope*(I - I_threshold), using the slope efficiency and drive current above the threshold current. Below threshold the laser emits negligible coherent light.
notes: Valid only when I is greater than I_threshold; the model is linear and ignores rollover (thermal saturation) at high current. Slope efficiency eta_slope is in watts of optical output per ampere of drive current.

name: Sound Pressure Level (SPL)
description: Computes the sound pressure level in decibels from a sound pressure p relative to a reference pressure pref. It is 20 times the base-10 logarithm of the pressure ratio, so each factor of ten in pressure adds 20 dB.
notes: The reference is normally 20 micropascals in air; both pressures are typically RMS values. Uses a factor of 20 (a field quantity), not 10 as for power.

name: Acoustic Beat Frequency
description: Returns the beat frequency heard when two tones of frequencies f1 and f2 sound together, equal to the absolute value of their difference. It is the rate at which the combined amplitude rises and falls.
notes: Beats are clearly perceived only when the two frequencies are close. The absolute value ensures a positive result regardless of which frequency is higher.

name: Vibrating String Fundamental Frequency
description: Gives the fundamental vibration frequency of a stretched string of length L under tension T with linear mass density mu. It is one over 2*L times the square root of tension divided by linear density.
notes: Assumes an ideal flexible string fixed at both ends with negligible stiffness. Linear density mu is mass per unit length in kg/m, not total mass.

name: Vibrating String Harmonic Frequency
description: Computes the frequency of the nth harmonic of a stretched string of length L under tension T with linear density mu. It equals n over 2*L times the square root of tension divided by linear density, so harmonics are integer multiples of the fundamental.
notes: Valid for an ideal string; real strings with stiffness show slightly sharp (inharmonic) upper partials. Harmonic number n must be a positive integer.

name: Open Pipe Resonance Frequency
description: Gives the nth resonance frequency of a pipe open at both ends, where sound speed is v and length is L. It is n*v divided by 2*L, so the pipe supports all integer harmonics of the fundamental.
notes: Ignores the end correction, which slightly lowers the true frequency for real open ends. Harmonic number n is a positive integer; sound speed v depends on air temperature.

name: Closed Pipe Resonance Frequency
description: Computes the resonance frequencies of a pipe closed at one end, using mode number n. It is (2*n-1)*v divided by 4*L, so only odd harmonics of the fundamental are present.
notes: The (2*n-1) factor gives 1, 3, 5 times the fundamental; even harmonics are absent. Ignores end correction and assumes a uniform pipe; v depends on temperature.

name: Sabine Reverberation Time
description: Estimates the RT60 reverberation time of a room using Sabine's formula, the time for sound to decay by 60 dB. It is 0.161 times the room volume V divided by the total absorption A in metric sabins.
notes: The constant 0.161 is for SI units (meters, seconds) at typical air conditions. Sabine's formula overestimates RT in highly absorptive rooms; use Eyring there instead.

name: Eyring-Norris Reverberation Time
description: Computes reverberation time using the Eyring-Norris formula, which corrects Sabine's for rooms with high average absorption. It is 0.161*V divided by the negative of surface area S times the natural log of one minus the mean absorption coefficient a.
notes: Mean absorption a is a fraction between 0 and 1, not a percent; a approaching 1 makes the log diverge. More accurate than Sabine when a is large.

name: Specific Acoustic Impedance
description: Gives the characteristic specific acoustic impedance of a medium, the product of its density rho and sound speed c. It relates sound pressure to particle velocity in a plane wave and characterizes the medium for reflection and transmission.
notes: This is the real characteristic impedance of a lossless medium for a plane wave; local impedance can differ near sources or boundaries. Air is about 415 Pa s/m at room conditions.

name: Acoustic Intensity from Pressure
description: Computes the acoustic intensity of a plane sound wave from its RMS pressure p, dividing the pressure squared by the medium impedance rho*c. The result is the time-averaged power carried per unit area.
notes: Valid for a plane progressive wave in a free field; use RMS, not peak, pressure. Density times sound speed is the medium's characteristic impedance.

name: Acoustic Particle Velocity
description: Gives the acoustic particle velocity in a plane wave, the oscillation speed of medium particles, by dividing the sound pressure p by the medium impedance rho*c. It links pressure and motion in the wave.
notes: Holds for a plane progressive wave where pressure and velocity are in phase; near sources they can differ in phase. This is particle velocity, not the sound speed c.

name: Mass Law Transmission Loss
description: Estimates the airborne sound transmission loss of a single limp panel using the mass law, from frequency f and surface (areal) density m. It is 20 times the log of f*m minus 47 dB, so loss rises about 6 dB per doubling of frequency or mass.
notes: An empirical normal-incidence approximation valid above the panel resonance and below the coincidence frequency; stiffness and damping are ignored. Surface density m is mass per unit area in kg/m^2.

name: Sound Power Level
description: Computes the sound power level in decibels of a source emitting acoustic power W relative to a reference power Wref. It is 10 times the base-10 logarithm of the power ratio, an absolute property of the source independent of distance.
notes: The standard reference is 1 picowatt; uses a factor of 10 because power is an energy quantity. Distinct from sound pressure level, which depends on distance and room.

name: Inverse-Square Sound Attenuation
description: Gives the drop in sound pressure level between two distances r1 and r2 from a point source in a free field. It is 20 times the log of r2 over r1, yielding about 6 dB of attenuation for each doubling of distance.
notes: Assumes free-field spherical spreading from a point source with no reflections or atmospheric absorption. The result is positive when r2 is greater than r1.

name: General Doppler Effect
description: Computes the frequency heard when both observer and source move along the line between them, from source frequency f0 and sound speed c. It multiplies f0 by (c+vo) over (c-vs), where vo is observer speed toward the source and vs is source speed toward the observer.
notes: Sign conventions matter: velocities are positive toward the other party; reverse signs for receding motion. Both speeds must stay below c, and this classical form assumes a still medium.

name: Temperature-Dependent Sound Speed (root)
description: Estimates the speed of sound in air as a function of Celsius temperature T, using the square-root scaling of speed with absolute temperature. It is 331.3 times the square root of one plus T divided by 273.15.
notes: Input temperature is in degrees Celsius, not kelvin; the formula converts internally. Valid for dry air; humidity and composition cause small deviations.

name: Standing Wave Wavelength (string)
description: Gives the wavelength of the nth standing-wave mode on a string of length L fixed at both ends. It is 2*L divided by the harmonic number n, since the string holds an integer number of half-wavelengths.
notes: Applies to a string fixed at both ends (nodes at each end); harmonic number n is a positive integer. This is a geometric result, independent of tension or density.

name: Helmholtz Resonator Frequency
description: Computes the resonance frequency of a Helmholtz resonator, a cavity of volume V with a neck of area A and length Lneck. It is c over 2*pi times the square root of A divided by V times Lneck, the natural frequency of the air plug oscillating against the cavity's springiness.
notes: Valid when wavelength is much larger than the resonator; use an effective neck length with end correction for accuracy. A is the neck cross-section, V the enclosed cavity volume.

name: Acoustic Pressure Reflection Coefficient
description: Gives the pressure reflection coefficient at a boundary between two media of acoustic impedances Z1 and Z2 for normal incidence. It is (Z2-Z1) divided by (Z2+Z1), the ratio of reflected to incident sound pressure.
notes: For normal incidence only; a negative value means a phase inversion on reflection. Impedances are characteristic (rho*c) values; magnitude near 1 indicates a strong mismatch.

name: Acoustic Intensity Transmission Coefficient
description: Computes the fraction of sound intensity transmitted across a boundary between media of impedances Z1 and Z2 at normal incidence. It is 4*Z1*Z2 divided by the square of (Z1+Z2), a value between 0 and 1.
notes: For normal incidence; it is symmetric in Z1 and Z2 and equals one minus the intensity reflection coefficient. A large impedance mismatch drives transmission toward zero.

name: Loudness in Sones (Stevens)
description: Converts a loudness level L in phons to loudness in sones using Stevens's relation, where a doubling of sones corresponds to a perceived doubling of loudness. It is 2 raised to the power (L-40)/10, giving 1 sone at 40 phons.
notes: Valid roughly above 40 phons; below this the relation deviates. Phons equal the SPL in dB of an equally loud 1 kHz tone, so L already encodes the equal-loudness contour.

name: Sound Wavelength
description: Gives the wavelength of a sound wave from the sound speed c and frequency f, as c divided by f. It is the spatial period, the distance between successive pressure maxima.
notes: Sound speed c depends on the medium and its temperature, so use the local value. Frequency and speed must use consistent SI units for a wavelength in meters.

name: Mach Cone Angle
description: Computes the half-angle of the Mach cone (shock wave) produced by an object moving supersonically at speed v, where sound speed is c. It is the arcsine of c divided by v, so faster objects make a narrower cone.
notes: Defined only for supersonic motion (v greater than c); otherwise the arcsine argument exceeds 1. The result is the half-angle in radians measured from the direction of travel.

name: Speed of Sound in Solid (rod)
description: Gives the speed of longitudinal sound waves along a thin solid rod, from its Young's modulus Ey and density rho. It is the square root of Ey divided by rho.
notes: Valid for a thin rod where lateral motion is unconstrained; bulk solids use elastic moduli that include Poisson effects and give higher speeds. Young's modulus is in pascals.

name: Newton-Laplace Sound Speed
description: Computes the speed of sound in a gas using the Newton-Laplace equation, from adiabatic index gamma, pressure P, and density rho. It is the square root of gamma*P divided by rho, treating sound propagation as an adiabatic process.
notes: Assumes an ideal gas with adiabatic (not isothermal) compression; gamma is dimensionless (about 1.4 for air). Because P over rho is fixed at given temperature, the speed depends mainly on temperature.

name: Decibel Sum of Two Sources
description: Combines two incoherent sound levels L1 and L2 into a single decibel level by summing their powers. It converts each level back to a power ratio, adds them, and takes 10 times the log of the total.
notes: Valid for uncorrelated sources adding on an energy basis; correlated sources can interfere and differ. Two equal levels combine to 3 dB more, not double the number.

name: Total Absorption Area
description: Gives the equivalent absorption area of a surface, the product of its area S and absorption coefficient a, measured in metric sabins. It quantifies how much sound energy the surface removes and feeds directly into reverberation-time calculations.
notes: Absorption coefficient a is a fraction between 0 and 1, not a percent. For a room, sum this product over all surfaces to obtain the total absorption A.

name: Rectangular Room Mode Frequency
description: Computes the frequency of an axial, tangential, or oblique acoustic mode in a rectangular room with dimensions Lx, Ly, Lz and mode indices nx, ny, nz. It is c over 2 times the root-sum-square of each index divided by its room dimension.
notes: Assumes rigid walls and an empty rectangular room; mode indices are non-negative integers (not all zero). Low-order modes set the room's problematic low-frequency resonances.

name: Ultrasound Doppler Shift
description: Gives the Doppler frequency shift measured in ultrasound when a transmitted beam of frequency f reflects off a target moving at velocity v, with sound speed c. It is 2*f*v*cos(theta) over c, where theta is the angle between the beam and the motion.
notes: The factor of 2 accounts for the round trip to and from the moving reflector; beam angle theta is in radians. Sensitivity vanishes as theta approaches 90 degrees where cosine is zero.

name: Acoustic Energy Density
description: Gives the acoustic energy density of a traveling plane wave, the sound energy stored per unit volume, by dividing the sound intensity I by the sound speed c. Intensity is energy density times propagation speed, so this inverts that relation.
notes: Valid for a plane progressive wave where energy travels at the sound speed; standing or reactive fields differ. Intensity I is in W/m^2 and sound speed c in m/s.

name: Critical Distance (Reverberation)
description: Estimates the critical (reverberation) distance from a source in a room, where the direct sound level equals the reverberant level. It is 0.057 times the square root of room volume V divided by reverberation time RT.
notes: An empirical relation for a diffuse field and omnidirectional source; the constant 0.057 assumes SI units. Beyond this distance the reverberant field dominates over direct sound.

name: Schroeder Frequency
description: Gives the Schroeder frequency of a room, the crossover above which room modes overlap densely enough to be treated statistically rather than individually. It is 2000 times the square root of reverberation time RT divided by room volume V.
notes: The constant 2000 assumes SI units (seconds, cubic meters). Below this frequency discrete modes dominate the acoustics; above it a diffuse-field description applies.

name: Panel Coincidence Frequency
description: Estimates the critical coincidence frequency of a flat panel, where the bending wavelength matches the airborne sound wavelength and transmission loss dips sharply. It is the air sound speed c squared divided by 1.8 times the panel's longitudinal wave speed cl times thickness h.
notes: An approximate relation with an empirical constant; near this frequency the mass law breaks down and sound leaks through. Thickness h is in meters and cl is the panel material's longitudinal speed.

name: Directivity Index
description: Converts a directivity factor Q into the directivity index in decibels, expressing how much a source concentrates sound in a preferred direction versus an omnidirectional radiator. It is 10 times the base-10 logarithm of Q.
notes: Q is dimensionless and at least 1; Q of 1 (omnidirectional) gives 0 dB, and each doubling adds about 3 dB. Q depends on frequency and the chosen direction.

name: Equivalent Absorption Area (from RT60)
description: Recovers a room's total equivalent absorption area from its measured reverberation time T and volume V, by inverting Sabine's formula. It is 0.161*V divided by T, expressed in metric sabins.
notes: Assumes Sabine conditions; the constant 0.161 is for SI units. This back-calculated absorption lets you predict how added absorptive treatment will change the reverberation time.

name: Equal-Tempered Frequency Ratio
description: Computes the frequency of a note that is n equal-tempered semitones above (or below) a base frequency f1. It multiplies f1 by 2 raised to n over 12, since twelve equal semitones span one octave (a factor of 2).
notes: Uses 12-tone equal temperament; n is signed, with negative values giving lower pitches. Non-integer n is allowed and yields microtonal intervals.

name: Musical Interval (cents)
description: Measures the size of a musical interval between two frequencies f2 and f1 in cents, where 100 cents is one equal-tempered semitone and 1200 cents is an octave. It is 1200 times the base-2 logarithm of the ratio f2 over f1.
notes: The result is signed: positive when f2 is higher, negative when lower. Cents are logarithmic, so equal cent values represent equal perceived pitch distances regardless of register.

name: Doppler Wavelength (moving source)
description: Gives the wavelength of sound ahead of a source moving toward the observer at speed vs, emitting frequency f0 in a medium of sound speed c. It is (c-vs) divided by f0, showing how forward motion compresses the wavefronts.
notes: For a source approaching, use vs positive; a receding source needs vs negative, which lengthens the wavelength. Source speed vs must remain below c to stay subsonic.

name: Sound Pressure from SPL
description: Recovers the sound pressure from a sound pressure level SPL in decibels, the inverse of the SPL formula. It multiplies the reference pressure pref by 10 raised to SPL over 20, giving the pressure in pascals.
notes: Uses a factor of 20 in the exponent because pressure is a field quantity; the reference is normally 20 micropascals in air. The result is typically an RMS pressure.

name: Atmospheric Absorption Loss
description: Computes the total sound attenuation from atmospheric absorption over a propagation distance d, given an absorption coefficient alpha in decibels per meter. It is simply alpha times d, the excess loss beyond geometric spreading.
notes: This adds to inverse-square spreading loss, not replaces it. The coefficient alpha depends strongly on frequency, temperature, and humidity, and is much larger at high frequencies.

name: Sound Level Distance Attenuation
description: Computes the sound pressure level at a distance r2 given the level L1 at reference distance r1, using L1 - 20*log(r2/r1). It applies inverse-square spreading of sound from a point source in free field.
notes: The 20*log term gives a 6 dB drop per doubling of distance for a point source; log is base-10. Assumes free-field spreading with no reflections, absorption, or barriers.

name: Sound Pressure Level
description: Computes the sound pressure level in decibels from a sound pressure p relative to a reference pressure p0, using 20*log(p/p0). It expresses acoustic pressure on the logarithmic dB scale.
notes: Pressures p and p0 share units and log is base-10; the standard reference p0 in air is 20 micropascals. The factor 20 (not 10) is used because level is defined from pressure amplitude, not power.

name: Combined Sound Level
description: Computes the total sound pressure level from two incoherent sources with individual levels L1 and L2, using 10*log(10^(L1/10) + 10^(L2/10)). Levels are combined by summing their energies, not by simple addition.
notes: Decibels cannot be added directly; energies (antilogs) are summed. Two equal levels combine to about 3 dB above one; log is base-10 and assumes uncorrelated sources.

name: Average Daylight Factor
description: Estimates the average ratio of indoor to outdoor daylight in a side-lit room (BRE formula).
notes: Above about 2 % a room feels daylit; 5 % bright.

name: Number of Luminaires (Lumen Method)
description: Gives how many luminaires a room needs to reach an average illuminance.
notes: Offices usually need 300–500 lx on the desk.

name: Room Cavity Ratio

variables.label: Height from work plane to luminaires

description: Characterises room shape for looking up the utilisation factor in lighting design.
notes: Tall narrow rooms have high ratios and waste more light on the walls.

name: Lighting Power Density
description: Gives installed lighting power per floor area, used in energy codes.
notes: Efficient LED offices reach about 5–8 W/m².

name: Noise Barrier Insertion Loss (Maekawa)

variables.label: Path length difference over the barrier

description: Gives the noise reduction of a barrier from the extra path length sound travels over it, via the Fresnel number N = 2δ/λ (Maekawa 1968).
notes: Low frequencies bend over barriers easily; practical barriers give 5–15 dB.

name: Sound Level in a Room (Direct + Reverberant)
description: Gives the sound pressure level at a distance in a room, combining direct sound and the reverberant field.
notes: Beyond the critical distance adding absorption helps; near the source it doesn't.

name: Vibration Velocity from Acceleration
description: Converts a sinusoidal vibration's acceleration into velocity amplitude, the quantity machinery vibration standards (ISO 10816) use.
notes: Divide again by 2πf for displacement.

name: Speed of Sound in Fresh Water (Marczak)
description: Gives the speed of sound in pure water at atmospheric pressure from 0 to 95 °C (Marczak 1997).
notes: About 1482 m/s at 20 °C — over four times faster than in air.

name: Wave Speed on a Stretched String
description: Gives the speed of transverse waves on a string or cable under tension.
notes: Tightening a guitar string raises its pitch because the wave speed rises.

name: Power Carried by a Wave on a String
description: Gives the average power transported by a sinusoidal wave on a string: ½μω²A²v.
notes: Power grows with the square of both frequency and amplitude.

name: Position of the n-th Node of a Standing Wave
description: Gives the distance of the n-th node from a fixed end; nodes are half a wavelength apart and antinodes lie halfway between.
notes: Used for microwave-oven and Kundt's-tube speed-of-light and sound experiments.

name: Radar Doppler Shift
description: Gives the frequency shift of a radar echo from a target moving at speed v; the factor 2 is because the wave travels out and back.
notes: A police K-band radar (24.125 GHz) sees about 161 Hz per km/h.

name: Echo Frequency from a Moving Reflector
description: Gives the frequency heard back from a wave reflected by an approaching object — used in sonar and bat echolocation.
notes: Use a negative speed for a receding reflector.

name: Fresnel Reflectance (s-Polarised)
expression: ((n1 * cos(rad(ti)) - n2 * sqrt(1 - (n1 / n2 * sin(rad(ti)))^2)) / (n1 * cos(rad(ti)) + n2 * sqrt(1 - (n1 / n2 * sin(rad(ti)))^2)))^2
description: Gives the fraction of s-polarised (perpendicular) light reflected at a flat interface at a given angle.
notes: Rises steadily to 1 at grazing incidence.

name: Fresnel Reflectance (p-Polarised)
expression: ((n1 * sqrt(1 - (n1 / n2 * sin(rad(ti)))^2) - n2 * cos(rad(ti))) / (n1 * sqrt(1 - (n1 / n2 * sin(rad(ti)))^2) + n2 * cos(rad(ti))))^2
description: Gives the fraction of p-polarised (parallel) light reflected at a given angle; it drops to zero at Brewster's angle.
notes: Polarised sunglasses exploit this: glare off water is mostly s-polarised.

name: Transmittance of a Clear Slab (Both Surfaces)
description: Gives the fraction of light passing through a non-absorbing plate at normal incidence, counting all multiple reflections between its two faces.
